adoption.body: Current AI use increased slightly to 23.8% of businesses, while expected use within six months rose to 27.6%. The gap narrowed to 3.8 percentage points, putting stated near-term intentions closer to reported deployment. Adoption remains uneven: the leading sector's current-use reading rose materially to 49.0%, more than twice the all-business rate.
adoption.headline: Business AI use rises as the near-term intention gap narrows

compute.body: Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, with capacity utilization at 81.7%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%, but utilization was lower at 72.2%. Output is rising in both industries, while the utilization gap indicates different pressure on installed capacity.
compute.headline: Compute output is growing under different capacity conditions

economic_impact.body: Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% as real output rose 2.5%. Real hourly compensation increased 0.6%, while unit labor costs grew 1.4%, indicating positive aggregate performance without a comparable increase in real compensation. A report that investors are pricing in a 32.6% AI productivity boost for software engineers describes an expectation for a specific workforce segment, not an economy-wide result. The current aggregate data do not identify AI's contribution.
economic_impact.headline: Productivity is rising, but compensation gains remain modest

grid_storage.body: Electric-power construction growth increased materially to 10.8%. The active interconnection queue stands at 2,061 GW, and only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages; storage accounts for 552.7 GW of the queue. S&P Global reports that data centers are adding to transmission congestion. Faster construction is a meaningful counterweight, but most requested capacity has not reached an advanced stage.
grid_storage.headline: Grid construction accelerates while most queued capacity remains at early stages

macro.body: Investor support remains constructive but selective. The AI Equity Index edged up to 36.7 and the median one-year return reached 13.7%, while the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns fell to 62.7%. The Financial Times reported that robust AI spending was supporting expectations for another strong U.S. earnings season, but the return data still show uneven participation. Financing is also mixed: the NFCI is -0.49 after a 0.02 rise over three months, while borrower strain is 26.0 and lender strain is -13.5. Computer and peripheral-equipment output is growing 9.2%, and semiconductor and electronic-component output 11.5%. Commercial electricity demand growth of 3.1% is also outpacing total retail demand growth of 1.2%. These are broad industry measures rather than AI-only series, but they describe an expanding hardware and power context for the buildout. Grid execution remains separate from the size of the pipeline: only 24.2% of the active interconnection queue is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Utility Dive reported that MISO proposed fast-track studies for large loads and generation. The proposal is a procedural change, not delivered capacity. Broader diffusion is less evident in labor and business use. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth, led by power and communication construction at 0.8%, and two have positive real-earnings growth. CNBC reported surging Wall Street AI hiring, which provides a sector-specific contrast rather than evidence of broad acceleration. Current AI use is reported by 23.8% of businesses, with 27.6% expecting use within six months. These measures leave diffusion through firms and the labor market incomplete even as selected industries report strong AI hiring.
macro.headline: Market support and physical expansion coexist with narrow labor gains

market.body: The AI Equity Index edged up to 36.7 and the median one-year return rose to 13.7%, but the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns slipped to 62.7%. Gains therefore persisted without becoming more broadly distributed. The Financial Times reported that robust AI spending was supporting expectations for another strong U.S. earnings season. That strengthens the near-term earnings narrative, but it does not show that results are improving across the full set of covered companies.
market.headline: AI shares advance without broader participation

power.body: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.1%, versus 1.2% for total retail demand, while retail prices are up 4.4%. Net planned generation additions total 225.2 GW through the pipeline horizon. Utility Dive reported that MISO proposed a fast-track study process for large loads and generation. The proposal concerns study timing; it does not establish when planned capacity will connect or how local supply-demand balances will change.
power.headline: Commercial demand leads electricity growth as faster grid studies are proposed

workforce.body: Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth. Power and communication construction leads at 0.8%, while two channels have positive real-earnings growth. CNBC reported that Wall Street AI hiring is surging, providing a sector-specific counterpoint. The report does not amount to broad acceleration across the tracked labor channels.
workforce.headline: Sector-specific AI hiring contrasts with narrow tracked job growth

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

body.text: The AI Equity Index rose slightly to 37.5, and the median one-year return increased materially to 15.6%. Yet the share of covered companies with positive one-year returns slipped to 62.3%. The typical covered return improved, but gains did not spread to a larger share of companies.

headline.text: AI equity returns improve without broader participation

body.text: Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2% with capacity utilization at 81.7%; semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5% with utilization at 72.2%. Computer equipment is operating closer to measured capacity even though semiconductor output is growing faster. The lower semiconductor utilization rate does not show that every stage of production is unconstrained: recent reports examined the move toward production control in advanced packaging and critical-defect detection in hybrid bonding. Those reports identify process execution and quality control as active issues beyond the aggregate utilization measure.

headline.text: Compute output grows as packaging reports focus on production control

body.text: Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.1%, ahead of the 1.2% increase in total retail demand, while retail prices are up 4.4%. Net planned generation additions total 225.2 GW through the pipeline horizon, but that total does not establish when capacity will become available. Utility Dive reported that Amazon and Constellation signed a 20-year power-purchase agreement to expand a Maryland nuclear plant. The agreement is a concrete long-duration supply arrangement, but one contract does not resolve broader questions about regional delivery and timing.

headline.text: Amazon signs a 20-year nuclear agreement as commercial power demand rises

body.text: PJM approved fast-track interconnection for 2.1 GW from Engie and LS Power, a concrete step for those projects. Systemwide, however, the active queue is 2,061 GW and only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Storage represents 552.7 GW of the queue. The historical record remains difficult: just 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. The approval advances selected projects, not the wider queue.

headline.text: PJM fast-tracks 2.1 GW against a 2,061 GW interconnection queue

body.text: Businesses expecting to use AI within six months rose slightly to 27.7%, while the gap between expected and current use widened slightly to 3.9 percentage points. Current-use readings now cover every BTOS sector, and the leading sector registers 50.2%. A separate 2025 Small Business Credit Survey found that 46% of firms with employees reported using AI tools and another 15% planned to adopt them within a year. Because that survey covers a different business population and time horizon, its higher readings should not be compared directly with BTOS.

headline.text: Near-term AI adoption expectations edge higher but remain ahead of use

body.text: Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth, and power and communication construction leads the group at 0.8%. Two channels have positive real-earnings growth. Reuters reported companies cutting jobs as investment shifts toward AI, while the Financial Times reported that economists remain unconvinced by broad claims of AI-driven job loss. The tracked measures show no broad employment growth, but they do not establish why the other channels are not growing.

headline.text: Employment growth remains narrow amid an unsettled AI job-loss debate

body.text: Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% and real output 2.5%, while real hourly compensation rose 0.6% and unit labor costs 1.4%. Barron's reported that heavy AI spending is supporting the economy while productivity gains from that investment may come later. The aggregate figures show positive productivity growth now, but they do not identify AI's contribution or show a comparable increase in real compensation.

headline.text: Productivity growth remains stronger than real compensation growth
Industrial expansion coexists with limited grid conversion and narrow job growth

paragraphs.text: Investor and industrial indicators remain supportive, though not uniformly so. The AI Equity Index rose slightly to 37.5 and the median one-year return reached 15.6%, while the share of covered companies with gains slipped to 62.3%. Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, and semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%. Those are broad manufacturing measures rather than AI-only series. Recent reports on advanced packaging's move toward production control and on hybrid-bonding defect detection show that manufacturing execution is receiving attention alongside output growth.

Power supply is drawing more concrete commitments, but delivery remains constrained. Commercial electricity demand is growing 3.1%, ahead of 1.2% total retail growth, and planned net generation additions stand at 225.2 GW. Utility Dive reported that Amazon and Constellation signed a 20-year agreement to expand a Maryland nuclear plant, while PJM approved fast-track interconnection for 2.1 GW from Engie and LS Power. Yet only 24.2% of the 2,061 GW active queue is in executed-agreement or construction stages, and just 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. The contract and approval advance specific projects; they do not indicate rapid conversion of the full pipeline.

Diffusion beyond the buildout remains uneven. Businesses expecting AI use within six months rose to 27.7%, 3.9 percentage points above current use. A separate survey found that 46% of firms with employees were using AI tools and another 15% planned to adopt them within a year, although the different population and time horizon prevent a direct comparison. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel had positive employment growth, led by power and communication construction at 0.8%. At the economy-wide level, productivity grew 2.2% and real output 2.5%, but real hourly compensation increased only 0.6%. These readings show positive aggregate performance, but not broad employment gains or a comparable rise in real compensation, and they do not isolate AI's contribution to productivity.
